title: Hubble portrays a dusty spiral galaxy
caption: The edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 4183, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 4183 · constellation Canes Venatici · about 55 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Seen edge-on against a backdrop of far-off galaxies and nearby stars, the spiral NGC 4183 shows off its disc, threaded with dark, intricate filaments of dust that block visible light from its core. It lies roughly 55 million light-years from the Sun in the northern constellation Canes Venatici, the Hunting Dogs, and belongs to the Ursa Major Group.

At about eighty thousand light-years across, it is a little smaller than the Milky Way. It has a faint core and an open spiral pattern, but from our viewing angle the arms are hard to appreciate. What we get instead is a clear look at the disc, which, like other galaxy discs, is built mostly of gas, dust and stars.

Recent studies suggest NGC 4183 may also have a bar. Bars are thought to funnel gas from the spiral arms toward the middle, boosting star formation there. Usually, new stars form more readily in the arms than in the central bulge.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.23 x 2.59 arcminutes) and distance (55 million light years), the frame spans roughly 52,000 × 41,000 light-years. Its light set out about 55 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys (Wide Field Channel) combined visible and infrared images. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the data is infrared light, invisible to the eye, and long exposures reveal far more than an eye could.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The British astronomer William Herschel was the first to observe NGC 4183. This picture combines visible and infrared images from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, covers a field about 3.4 arcminutes wide, and draws on data that Luca Limatola identified for Hubble's Hidden Treasures, a contest in image processing.
alt: An edge-on spiral galaxy with dark, intricate dust filaments along its disc, set against distant galaxies and nearby stars.
